item.aggregated_output:
<<22:5 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
22:5/q01 Who is addressed by 'O people'?  [ٱلنَّاسُ · referent] (turns on: Whether the general wording primarily addresses Meccan deniers or all people.)
  22:5/q01/p1 The unbelievers or polytheists of Mecca, especially resurrection deniers. — reasons: Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās via Wāḥidī, and others identify the Meccan audience; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they are the primary target, while the wording remains general.
  22:5/q01/p2 The wording addresses people generally, while deniers are especially in view. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī preserves the general wording; Biqāʿī allows both scopes and associates the broad address with prevalence of denial.
22:5/q02 Why frame the doubt with 'if'? [إِن كُنتُمْ فِى رَيْبٍۢ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the condition depicts entrenched doubt, weak doubt, or accommodates a mixed audience.)
  22:5/q02/p1 It poses actual doubt hypothetically so the proof can dispel or rebuke it. — reasons: Bursevī says the evidence uproots doubt; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 43:5; Ālūsī says the condition ascribes doubt to deniers without strengthening their case.
22:5/q03 What does rayb mean here? [رَيْبٍۢ · meaning] (turns on: Whether it is plain doubt or doubt colored by disturbance, suspicion, or fear.)
  22:5/q03/p1 Doubt about resurrection. — reasons: Yaḥyā, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Ibn ʿAbbās use the ordinary gloss; Qurṭubī also records accusation and need in other contexts.
  22:5/q03/p2 A troubling, ugly doubt, with possible fear or suspicion. — reasons: Ṭabrisī calls it an ugly doubt; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues rayb and shakk are not synonyms, citing Qurʾānic distribution, lexicographers, and poetry; Ibn Fāris adds fear.
22:5/q04 What aspect of resurrection is doubted? [مِّنَ ٱلْبَعْثِ · interpretation] (turns on: Possibility or actual occurrence.)
  22:5/q04/p1 Whether reviving the dead is possible and within divine power. — reasons: Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī emphasize possibility because the following creation proofs show capacity; Ālūsī cites 22:7 for occurrence.
  22:5/q04/p2 Whether resurrection will in fact occur. — reasons: Bursevī notes this alternative; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it return to God; Islāḥī explains idolaters' reluctance to face accountability.
22:5/q05 How is البعث read? [ٱلْبَعْثِ · readings] (turns on: Whether ʿayn is quiescent or open, and whether vowel alternation is a general guttural rule or only attested usage.)
  22:5/q05/p1 The usual reading has quiescent ʿayn. — reasons: Basrans treat open forms as lexical dialect variants; Kufans permit lightening around gutturals, a generalization contested by Abū Isḥāq and al-Samīn.
  22:5/q05/p2 Al-Ḥasan reads with open ʿayn. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and later commentators compare other guttural-middle words; Basrans call it dialectal, Kufans a lightening pattern.
22:5/q06 How does 'We created you' answer the condition? [فَإِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم · grammar] (turns on: Whether the clause itself is the answer or evidence for an omitted answer.)
  22:5/q06/p1 Creation is evidence for an implicit command to consider one's origin and recognize resurrection. — reasons: Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr note that creation preceded the hearers' doubt, so the literal act of creation cannot be a consequent event; Ālūsī permits the clause to occupy the answer's place.
  22:5/q06/p2 The creation clause directly presents the proof that resolves the conditional doubt. — reasons: Ṭabarī and others present the staged first creation as the immediate argument; the one who originated life can restore it.
22:5/q07 How were humans created from dust? [تُرَابٍۢ · referent] (turns on: Whether dust refers to Adam's origin or to the food-chain origin of every human.)
  22:5/q07/p1 It refers to Adam, ancestor of humankind, with descendants included through him. — reasons: Zajjāj, Ṭabarī and most commentators name Adam; Rāzī cites 3:59 and 20:55; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes Eve and later reproductive descent; Ālūsī prefers this.
  22:5/q07/p2 Each person derives from earth through nourishment, which becomes reproductive fluid and bodily matter. — reasons: Rāzī traces semen and menstrual blood through food to plants, earth and water; Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān give the same route; Study Quran includes animals and milk.
  22:5/q07/p3 Dust signals humanity's lowly biological kinship with earthy substances. — reasons: Asad cites 3:59 and 23:12; Muqātil recalls that humans began as nothing.
22:5/q08 What is a nutfah here? [نُّطْفَةٍۢ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the fluid is semen, Adam's own semen, or a fertilized ovum; its base water sense varies.)
  22:5/q08/p1 Semen from which Adam's descendants develop, literally a drop or quantity of water. — reasons: Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī and Ālūsī discuss dripping, flowing, or pouring roots; Ṭabrisī includes male and female fluid; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says water may be little or much.
  22:5/q08/p2 Adam's own semen is the intended drop. — reasons: Al-Naqqāsh is quoted by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān; Ālūsī calls this remote.
  22:5/q08/p3 It may name the sperm or the fertilized ovum produced from it. — reasons: Kur'an Yolu uses embryonic context; Elmalılı speaks more precisely of the seed within semen.
22:5/q09 What is an ʿalaqah? [عَلَقَةٍۢ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the word describes congealed blood or an attached early embryo.)
  22:5/q09/p1 A piece of fresh, thick, congealed or clotted blood. — reasons: Abū ʿUbayd emphasizes intense redness; Wāḥidī cites al-Qaṭāmī; al-Samīn cites an Arabic saying about battlefield blood; commentators describe the preceding fluid thickening.
  22:5/q09/p2 It denotes a moist, clinging or attached early stage. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī derives it from adhesion; Islāḥī allows a living leech-like referent; Kur'an Yolu prefers a fertilized ovum attached to the uterine wall.
22:5/q10 What is a muḍghah? [مُّضْغَةٍۢ · meaning]
  22:5/q10/p1 A small piece of flesh about the size of a mouthful to chew. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba compares names for scooped or eaten quantities; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains its morphology; a hadith calls the heart a muḍghah.
22:5/q11 What distinguishes formed from unformed? [مُّخَلَّقَةٍۢ غَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the contrast concerns form, completeness, ensoulment, miscarriage, term birth, or the primordial covenant.)
  22:5/q11/p1 One embryo is visibly shaped, complete or smooth; the other is not yet or imperfectly shaped. — reasons: Qatāda's complete/incomplete gloss is widespread. Zajjāj, Rāzī, Zamakhsharī, and Nasafī allow deficiencies in limbs and faculties; Rāzī prefers this because the address concerns future humans.
  22:5/q11/p2 The formed pregnancy lives or reaches birth; the unformed one miscarries before completion. — reasons: Mujāhid sometimes describes formed and unformed miscarriages; Ibn Masʿūd's angel report has an unformed drop expelled as blood. Ṭabarī prefers expulsion before completed shaping and ensoulment.
  22:5/q11/p3 The formed receives a spirit; the unformed lacks ensoulment. — reasons: Wāḥidī prefers this explanation, and Ibn ʿAbbās links it to life and the widow's waiting period; Bursevī reports an inward version in which unformed is an image without soul.
  22:5/q11/p4 The formed has the primordial covenant; the unformed does not. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās in ʿAṭāʾ's transmission and a report from Abū Jaʿfar identify formed particles in Adam's loins under the covenant; the latter includes expelled semen and pre-ensoulment miscarriage among unformed.
  22:5/q11/p5 Every developmental stage is created and may count as mukhallaqah. — reasons: Ibn al-ʿArabī reasons from the root; Qurṭubī prefers repeated creation and cites 23:14, against a sense restricted to an imaged fetus.
22:5/q12 How are the adjectives 'formed and unformed' construed or read? [مُّخَلَّقَةٍۢ غَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍۢ · readings] (turns on: Whether they are genitive adjectives or accusative circumstantial expressions.)
  22:5/q12/p1 The common genitive forms modify muḍghah. — reasons: Bursevī and Ālūsī make the attachment explicit; al-Samīn identifies the general reading.
  22:5/q12/p2 Accusative forms are read as circumstantial or detached qualifiers. — reasons: Al-Kisāʾī permits them; Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads both accusative; Sībawayh allows a circumstantial qualifier even after an indefinite noun, though rare.
22:5/q13 What do reports say about fetal stages and angelic decrees? [نُّطْفَةٍۢ عَلَقَةٍۢ مُّضْغَةٍۢ · reports] (turns on: The reports differ on the timing of shaping and angelic writing.)
  22:5/q13/p1 A drop, clot, and morsel each last forty days, followed by ensoulment and decrees. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd's Prophetic report lists provision, life, deeds, and fortune; Qurṭubī derives four months and links it to the widow's waiting period. Ibn Kathīr transmits Ṣaḥīḥayn versions.
  22:5/q13/p2 An angel shapes or records the embryo after roughly forty to forty-five nights. — reasons: Abū Dharr and Ḥudhayfa versions mention sex and fortune or bodily features; Ibn Kathīr cites Muslim. Bursevī says an early reference to form means its decree, with visible form later.
  22:5/q13/p3 A settled drop is classified as formed or expelled, and the formed child's particulars are copied from the Mother Book. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd and related reports list sex, provision, lifespan, deeds, fortune, and sometimes burial place; Ṭabāṭabāʾ reconciles changeable and unchangeable tablets.
22:5/q14 What does 'so that We may make clear to you' disclose? [لِّنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether its object is creation, power, resurrection, guidance, or intentionally left open.)
  22:5/q14/p1 The successive stages and manner of creation in wombs. — reasons: Yaḥyā, Ibn Qutayba, Wāḥidī's Ibn Muslim, and Qatāda focus on explaining the stages of human creation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports that incomplete embryos and miscarriages make womb stages clear.
  22:5/q14/p2 God's power, wisdom, and choice in creating varied forms. — reasons: Naḥḥās and Qurṭubī say the stages display divine power; Biqāʿī

<<22:5 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
argues variation defeats nature as a sufficient cause; Rāzī and Elmalılı add God's free choice.
  22:5/q14/p3 The truth or possibility of resurrection. — reasons: The author of al-Naẓm and Bursevī read the stages as disclosure of resurrection; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the clause parenthetical; Kur'an Yolu prefers gradual development as the fit with the passage.
  22:5/q14/p4 What people should do, avoid, and practice in worship. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās gives this gloss; Zajjāj connects human creation with guidance and right conduct.
  22:5/q14/p5 The object is omitted to suggest knowledge and signs beyond enumeration. — reasons: Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, and Ālūsī emphasize breadth; Ālūsī prefers this over restricting the object to resurrection.
22:5/q15 How is لنبين read? [لِّنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ · readings] (turns on: First-person nūn or third-person yāʾ.)
  22:5/q15/p1 The common reading uses nūn: 'so that We make clear.' — reasons: Rāzī and later grammarians contrast this with third-person variants.
  22:5/q15/p2 Ibn Abī ʿAblah and others read with yāʾ: 'so that He make clear.' — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī also names Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī; Ālūsī calls it a shift in grammatical person.
22:5/q16 How is ونقر read and connected syntactically? [وَنُقِرُّ · readings] (turns on: Indicative independent clause or accusative purpose; variant yāʾ and pouring-root forms.)
  22:5/q16/p1 The majority read indicative nuqirru, a new statement about retaining embryos. — reasons: Sībawayh, Farrāʾ, Zajjāj and others separate it from the purpose clause; Zajjāj argues humans were created for guidance, not simply retention; Kashf prefers coordination with 'We created.'
  22:5/q16/p2 An accusative/subjunctive reading coordinates retention, sometimes delivery, with 'to make clear.' — reasons: Transmitted from ʿĀṣim or Yaʿqūb; Zamakhsharī takes retention through birth and accountability as a second purpose; Abū al-Baqāʾ proposes an outcome lām, challenged by al-Samīn.
  22:5/q16/p3 Third-person variants use يقر or يُقر, with indicative or accusative endings. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Rajāʾ, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī are named; some yāʾ variants also govern يخرجكم.
  22:5/q16/p4 Yaʿqūb's نَقَرُّ derives from pouring water. — reasons: Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī distinguish the open nūn and ḍamma on qāf from the usual retention verb.
22:5/q17 What is kept in the womb, and until when? [وَنُقِرُّ فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ مَا نَشَآءُ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍۢ مُّسَمًّۭى · interpretation] (turns on: Whether retention means avoiding miscarriage, completing formation, or fulfilling an assigned lifespan.)
  22:5/q17/p1 God retains selected pregnancies to completed birth rather than allowing miscarriage. — reasons: Mujāhid glosses completion; Ibn Zayd says stay until emergence; several sources give six months as a minimum and differing maximums. Islāḥī stresses God's choice of sex and form.
  22:5/q17/p2 Retention lasts until the embryo completes formation. — reasons: Ṭabrisī reports Mujāhid's gloss; some accounts tie the term to individual fetal development.
  22:5/q17/p3 The phrase includes whoever is assigned a specified lifespan. — reasons: Ṭabrisī offers this alternative; Ṭabarī mentions God's decree of life to a fixed term.
22:5/q18 What is the appointed term, and what gestation lengths are reported? [أَجَلٍۢ مُّسَمًّۭى · interpretation] (turns on: The term is birth, but reports differ on maximum gestation.)
  22:5/q18/p1 The term is delivery; gestation varies, with six months often given as the minimum. — reasons: Wāḥidī and Bayḍāwī allow up to four years; Bursevī cites Abū Ḥanīfa's two, Shāfiʿī's four, and Mālik's five years, with anecdotes of prolonged pregnancies. Ibn ʿĀshūr says usual gestation is nine months nine days.
22:5/q19 How are ما نشاء and its pronoun read or chosen? [مَا نَشَآءُ · readings]
  22:5/q19/p1 The ordinary form uses nūn with fatḥa. — reasons: The wording mā covers pregnancy including the inanimate morsel, as Qurṭubī notes; Biqāʿī and Islāḥī stress God's choice of which fetus continues.
  22:5/q19/p2 Ibn Waththāb reads the nūn with kasra. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī transmit this vocalization.
22:5/q20 Why is طفل singular, and what does it mean? [طِفْلًۭا · grammar] (turns on: Generic or distributive singular, verbal noun, or singular licensed by the plural suffix.)
  22:5/q20/p1 A generic or distributive singular stands for children or each child. — reasons: Abū ʿUbayda cites poetry and 66:4; al-Samīn and Rāzī allow each of you; Samarrāʾī says the verse treats the human species; the noun generally covers birth to puberty.
  22:5/q20/p2 The singular functions as a verbal noun, applicable to one or many. — reasons: Ibn Jurayj compares ʿadl and zawr; al-Mubarrad cites 24:31; Wāḥidī discusses verbal-noun and specification parses; Ṭabarī is reported with specification.
  22:5/q20/p3 The plural object suffix already indicates a group, making a plural predicate unnecessary. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī reports this distinct grammatical account; al-Suyūṭī transmits an elided distributive repetition.
22:5/q21 What are the lexical limits and related uses of طفل? [طِفْلًۭا · meaning]
  22:5/q21/p1 A tender young child, usually from birth to puberty; related roots have several senses. — reasons: Abū al-Haytham and Qurṭubī discuss gender and number; Qurṭubī and al-Samīn add delicate, afternoon, rain, and animal-young uses, with poetry.
22:5/q22 How does ثم لتبلغوا connect to the preceding clause? [ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوٓا۟ أَشُدَّكُمْ · grammar] (turns on: A purpose of delivery, an omitted verb, an added thumma, or a purpose tied to womb retention.)
  22:5/q22/p1 Reaching maturity is the purpose of bringing children out and raising them. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr defends the causal lām and rejects alternatives; Kur'an Yolu prefers causality; Ālūsī says the repeated lām emphasizes responsibility.
  22:5/q22/p2 An omitted verb supplies 'then We let you live or grow' before the purpose clause. — reasons: The author of al-Naẓm, Ālūsī and Islāḥī supply the intervening development.
  22:5/q22/p3 Thumma is additional or functions like a simple conjunction. — reasons: Al-Naẓm and Qurṭubī record this, comparing 39:73; Ibn ʿĀshūr instead treats thumma as marking rank or reinforcing the earlier sequence.
  22:5/q22/p4 Maturity may be the aim of womb retention and delivery. — reasons: Al-Ṭībī allows this; Ālūsī rejects coordination directly with li-nubayyina as spoiling the structure.
22:5/q23 What is reaching full strength, and when does it occur? [أَشُدَّكُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Puberty, broader complete strength, and reported numerical ages.)
  22:5/q23/p1 It is complete physical strength, intellect, and discernment. — reasons: Zajjāj sets it between thirty and forty; other sources mention eighteen, thirty-two, thirty-six, forty, forty-five. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it youth with gathered capacities.
  22:5/q23/p2 It is the onset of puberty or sexual maturity. — reasons: Yaḥyā gives this gloss, and Ṭabrisī offers it as an alternative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verse may refer to orphan puberty.
22:5/q24 What is the grammatical form of أشد? [أَشُدَّكُمْ · grammar] (turns on: A plural with no used singular or a plural of shiddah.)
  22:5/q24/p1 It is a plural-like form with no ordinary singular. — reasons: Zamakhsharī suggests multiple aspects of strength; Nasafī repeats the form; Ālūsī surveys proposals.
  22:5/q24/p2 It is analyzed as a plural of shiddah. — reasons: Bayḍāwī compares anʿām from niʿmah; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī report the analysis.
22:5/q25 When do some people die relative to maturity and old age? [وَمِنكُم مَّن يُتَوَفَّىٰ · interpretation] (turns on: Before maturity, at or after maturity, or simply before senility.)
  22:5/q25/p1 Some die before reaching maturity. — reasons: Yaḥyā compares 40:67; Ibn ʿAbbās and many later commentators supply this implied timing; Islāḥī includes childhood and adolescence.
  22:5/q25/p2 Some die before reaching decrepit old age, including at or after maturity. — reasons: Māwardī, Baghawī and Ṭabāṭabāʾ infer contrast with the return to old age; Rāzī specifies death at full strength; Ālūsī objects to a circumstantial parse that forces death exactly at maturity.
22:5/q26 How is يتوفى read or construed? [يُتَوَفَّىٰ · readings] (turns on: Passive taking of life versus active completion or divine taking.)
  22:5/q26/p1 The usual passive form means a person is taken at death. — reasons: Bursevī identifies death and taking of the soul; Ālūsī says the passive leaves the understood divine agent unspoken.
  22:5/q26/p2 An active variant takes God as subject and the person as object. — reasons: Abū Ḥātim transmits it; al-Samīn and Ālūsī give this parse.
  22:5/q26/p3 An active variant takes the person as subject, meaning fulfillment of a lifespan. — reasons: Naḥḥās reports Abū Isḥāq; al-Samīn compares 2:234; Ālūsī records the same.
22:5/q27 What is the most decrepit age? [أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether it names senility generally or a fixed age.)
  22:5/q27/p1 Senile old age with bodily weakness and reduced intellect; no fixed onset. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects a rigid 75-year threshold because many remain sound at eighty; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī likewise note variation. Ṭabrisī says decline is worse than childhood weakness because childhood may improve.
  22:5/q27/p2 It begins at a reported numerical age, seventy-five or one hundred. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya questions the report of seventy-five from ʿAlī; a report attributed to al-Ṣādiq says one hundred.
22:5/q28 What does knowing nothing after knowledge mean? [لِكَيْلَا يَعْلَمَ مِنۢ بَعْدِ عِلْمٍۢ شَيْـًۭٔا · interpretation] (turns on: Loss of past knowledge, inability to learn, loss of action, or rhetorical overstatement.)
  22:5/q28/p1 The elderly person forgets former knowledge and loses understanding, sometimes described emphatically as knowing nothing. — reasons: Zamakhsharī describes repeated forgetting; Rāzī says the

<<22:5 update 1, part 2 of 0..4>>
absolute negation intensifies loss though some knowledge remains; Islāḥī prefers that even little acquired knowledge is erased, citing 17:85.
  22:5/q28/p2 The person can no longer acquire new knowledge and forgets what was learned. — reasons: Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Nasafī, and Abū Ḥayyān record this twofold interpretation.
  22:5/q28/p3 The person loses the ability to act after knowing. — reasons: Māwardī prefers this because old age harms action more visibly than knowledge, and action depends on knowing.
22:5/q29 Are Qurʾān readers or believers spared this decline? [أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ · interpretation] (turns on: Reports invoking 95:5–6 against Rāzī's reading of that passage.)
  22:5/q29/p1 Qurʾān readers, or people strengthened by faith, may be spared decrepit loss. — reasons: ʿIkrima and Ibn ʿAbbās cite the exception in 95:5–6; ʿAbd al-Malik says reciters retain intellect longest; Study Quran reports a faith version.
  22:5/q29/p2 The exception in 95:5–6 concerns believers' lasting reward, not exemption from senility. — reasons: Rāzī rejects a literal exemption from old age, reading the return to the lowest state as blame or punishment countered by reward.
22:5/q30 What inward meanings are given to bodily decline and earth's revival? [أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ ٱلْأَرْضَ هَامِدَةًۭ · inward] (turns on: Different spiritual analogies.)
  22:5/q30/p1 The worst age images spiritual stagnation, veiling, desire, self-reliance, or estrangement from God. — reasons: Qushayrī records distinct glosses: stagnation after striving, veiling after witnessing, returning to desires, disobedience, abasement, adversaries, ignorance of one's worth, self-reliance, and illusion of independence. Baqlī adds interruption after communion.
  22:5/q30/p2 The lifeless earth images an ignorant soul revived by knowledge and spiritual virtues. — reasons: Wāsiṭī says God revives humans here by knowledge and after death by spirits; Qāshānī interprets water as knowledge descending from the spirit.
  22:5/q30/p3 Created beings emerge from the wombs of nonexistence at a divinely appointed term. — reasons: The Najmī inward reading transfers gestation imagery to all creation; Bursevī connects it to eternal divine will and gradual perfection.
22:5/q31 Why does the verse turn from human development to the earth? [وَتَرَى ٱلْأَرْضَ · links] (turns on: How the second sign relates to the first and why the address shifts.)
  22:5/q31/p1 Reviving visible dead land supplies another analogy for bodily resurrection. — reasons: Qushayrī invokes spring; Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts unseen origin with visible growth; Abū Ḥayyān says the second proof is directly observable; several link it to the coming Hour in 22:6–7.
  22:5/q31/p2 The singular 'you see' invites any observer to inspect an outward sign. — reasons: Wāḥidī says the shift can mark a separate passage still linked by resurrection; Biqāʿī and Ālūsī address each suitable observer.
22:5/q32 What water is sent down on the earth? [ٱلْمَآءَ · referent] (turns on: Rain alone or rain and other irrigation.)
  22:5/q32/p1 Rain is the immediate referent. — reasons: Ṭabrisī states this; Ālūsī prefers rain because the text says it is sent down; Biqāʿī stresses its descent by divine power.
  22:5/q32/p2 Water also includes rivers, springs, and irrigation. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān broadens the referent; Ālūsī reports that possibility.
22:5/q33 What does hāmidah describe? [هَامِدَةًۭ · meaning] (turns on: Dry barren land, worn-out land, dust, or literally extinguished ash.)
  22:5/q33/p1 Dry, lifeless, barren earth with no vegetation. — reasons: Lexicographers compare an extinguished fire; al-Layth adds hard crust and Shammar settled ash. Ibn ʿAbbās mentions lost moisture; al-Aʿshā's worn-clothes verse attests the root.
  22:5/q33/p2 It means dusty, gray, or crumbling land. — reasons: Qatāda, Ibn Kathīr and al-Itqān specify the earth's dusty or broken appearance.
  22:5/q33/p3 It depicts the earth literally as extinguished ash from an earlier burning state. — reasons: Elmalılı prefers this over summer-dried soil and invokes contemporary theories of earth as hardened deposited ash; Kur'an Yolu reports his claim.
22:5/q34 What moves when the watered earth اهتزت? [ٱهْتَزَّتْ · interpretation] (turns on: The land's soil, its plants by metonymy, or an inverted event order.)
